The Caspian Spirlin Alburnoides eichwaldii ShirAbad, a cyprinid endemic to the ShirAbad River basin in Iran, exhibits life-history traits characteristic of small-bodied riverine leuciscids. Fertilised ova, measuring approximately 1.8 mm in diameter, are demersal and adhesive, adhering to submerged gravel during the incubation period. At the moment of emergence from the chorion, the prolarvae are remarkably diminutive, with newly hatched individuals measuring just 0.5 cm [Lb = 0.5 cm] in total length. The initial wet weight at birth, calculated from the spherical egg volume, is approximately 0.0031 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0031 grams], a mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. The larval eclosion event, occurring at a constant water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], is completed after a brief incubation of only 3 days , a rapid developmental rate that is consistent with observations in the congeneric Alburnoides bipunctatus.

After hatching, the yolk-sac larvae remain in a lecithotrophic state for a short period before the mouth opens and the digestive tract becomes functional. Under the same thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the transition to free-swimming and the commencement of first exogenous feeding occurs at approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] of age. This age at birth from the perspective of independent feeding is comparatively brief, likely an adaptation to the seasonal and often unpredictable flow regimes of the ShirAbad River. The rapid yolk absorption and early onset of active feeding allow the prolarvae to exploit the spring plankton bloom, maximising early growth potential. The progression from the yolk-sac stage to the exogenously feeding larva is a critical period of high mortality, and the short duration of this endotrophic window may serve to reduce the risk of starvation during a vulnerable phase when the larva is entirely dependent on its finite internal nutrient supply.

Sexual maturation in this species displays a pronounced sexual dimorphism in both timing and body size. Females attain gonadal puberty at a total length of 8.54 cm [Lp = 8.54 cm], which corresponds to a significantly older age of 2 years after birth [tp = 2 years after birth] when reared under controlled conditions at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. Males, in contrast, reach reproductive maturity at a larger body size of 9.64 cm [Lp = 9.64 cm] but do so after a much shorter period, achieving puberty at only 1 year after birth [tp = 1 year after birth] at the same thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This pattern suggests that males prioritise rapid attainment of reproductive capability, potentially to compete for access to spawning females early in the season, while females delay maturation in order to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves to support vitellogenesis and egg production. The divergence in these life-history schedules has significant implications for the operational sex ratio within the breeding population.

The maximum reproductive output for this species has been characterised under optimal thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females achieve a daily fecundity of approximately 22 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 22 eggs per day], a figure derived from field estimates of annual fecundity reflecting a batch-spawning strategy that produces multiple clutches over the spawning season. The ultimate total length recorded for adult individuals is 12.47 cm [Li = 12.47 cm], indicating that the species achieves a relatively modest maximum body size compared to other members of the genus. This asymptotic length, combined with the observed batch-fecundity strategy, positions Alburnoides eichwaldii ShirAbad as an opportunistic strategist, capable of rapidly colonising available habitat when conditions are favourable.

Longevity in the Caspian Spirlin is constrained by its small body size and the energetic demands of a high reproductive rate. The maximum lifespan recorded for individuals under stable laboratory conditions at a temperature regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] is approximately 1,095 days [am = approximately 1,095 days], equivalent to roughly 3 years. This relatively short lifespan, typical of small-bodied cyprinids, is punctuated by a single or at most two breeding seasons for the majority of survivors. Post-reproductive mortality is high, with many adults displaying signs of physiological senescence immediately after the final spawning event of the season. The species thus exhibits a life-history strategy that balances early maturity, high fecundity, and a brief adult lifespan, an adaptive syndrome that is well suited to the dynamic and sometimes ephemeral habitats of the ShirAbad drainage system, where environmental stochasticity favours rapid turnover and high annual reproductive investment over extended survival.
